paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Modern cities depend on what lies beneath their streets. Metro lines, sewers, water mains and power cables all need tunnels, and as cities grow, those tunnels must be longer, deeper and more numerous. In the past, many were built by a method known as cut-and-cover: workers dug a deep trench along a street, built the tunnel inside it and then covered it over again. The method is simple, but it closes roads and disturbs businesses for months or even years. Today, most urban tunnels are dug instead by tunnel-boring machines, huge mechanical moles that work entirely underground and leave life on the surface largely undisturbed.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: At the front of every tunnel-boring machine is a circular cutting head, whose diameter matches that of the finished tunnel: anything from two metres for a small sewer to more than fifteen metres for a road tunnel. The cutting head rotates slowly, perhaps two to five times a minute, while being pressed hard against the ground in front of it. Its tools depend on what it must dig through. In hard rock, it is fitted with disc cutters, rings of hardened steel that roll across the rock face under enormous force, causing it to crack into small chips. In softer ground such as clay or sand, scraping tools resembling teeth are used instead.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Most cities, however, are built on soft, wet ground, where the greatest danger is not that the machine will be unable to cut but that the ground in front of it will collapse into the tunnel, causing the surface above to sink. To prevent this, engineers often use an earth pressure balance machine. Here, the soil that has just been dug out is not removed at once but packed into a sealed chamber directly behind the cutting head. The pressure of this soil pushes back against the ground ahead and holds it in place, while a long screw conveyor removes soil from the chamber at a carefully controlled rate. In very loose or waterlogged ground, a slurry machine may be chosen instead. Its chamber is filled with a mixture of water and a fine clay called bentonite, which supports the ground ahead and also carries the excavated material up to the surface through pipes. There, the material is separated out, and the slurry is cleaned and pumped back down to be used again.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The machine moves forward in a repeated cycle. Large hydraulic rams arranged around the inside of the machine push against the most recently completed section of tunnel lining, driving the cutting head into the ground. Once the machine has advanced by about one and a half metres, the rams are drawn back and a mechanical arm called an erector picks up curved concrete segments, which are made in a factory on the surface, and fits them together to form a complete ring. Rubber seals between the segments keep water out. Finally, the narrow space left between the outside of the ring and the surrounding earth is filled with grout, a liquid mixture of cement and water that soon hardens, so that the ground has no room to move. On a good day in soft ground, the whole cycle may be repeated a dozen times or more.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Behind the cutting head stretches a chain of platforms known as the back-up, which may make a machine well over 100 metres long. It carries the control cabin, electrical equipment, the grout supply and a conveyor belt that takes away the excavated material. The machine is steered by a pilot in the control cabin, who relies on a laser guidance system: a laser fixed to the tunnel wall further back sends a beam to a target on the machine, and a computer shows how far it has strayed from its planned route, often to within a few millimetres. One of the hardest jobs is replacing worn cutters. In soft ground this may mean working inside the pressurised chamber, which is uncomfortable and dangerous, so manufacturers have begun to fit robotic arms that can change cutters without anyone entering the space.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Even with the best machines, a small amount of ground movement is almost unavoidable. Before work begins, engineers survey the buildings along the route and fix instruments to many of them to detect even slight movements. Sofia Brandt, who managed tunnelling on a recent metro extension, explains that her team received readings every few minutes and could adjust the pressure in the machine's chamber if the ground began to move. Where historic buildings were at risk, they also used a technique called compensation grouting, injecting grout into the soil beneath the foundations to make up for ground that had sunk. 'Most people living above the line,' she says, 'never knew we had passed underneath.'

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Tunnelling also has its traditions. Each machine is given a name before it starts work, usually a woman's name, and many crews place a small statue of Saint Barbara, the patron saint of miners and tunnellers, at the entrance to the tunnel. When a machine finally breaks through into the shaft at the end of its route, it is usually taken apart and lifted out in pieces. Occasionally, however, it is simply left buried, because removing it would cost more than the machine is worth.
